title: Udon Thani 2 Days 1 Night: City, Nong Prajak & Ban Chiang
metaDesc: A 2-day, 1-night Udon Thani plan in Thailand: stroll Nong Prajak and the giant yellow ducks, eat Vietnamese breakfast, then visit the Ban Chiang World Heritage site. Hour-by-hour, with budget and real spots.
keywords: Udon Thani 2 days 1 night, Udon Thani itinerary, Nong Prajak, Ban Chiang, things to do in Udon Thani
h1:
Udon Thani in 2 Days 1 Night
City, Nong Prajak & Ban Chiang
intro: Udon Thani is easier to enjoy than you'd expect. The city center is compact, an evening walk around Nong Prajak works for the whole family, and the next morning you drive out to Ban Chiang, the World Heritage archaeological site that travelers come from all over to see. This plan fits neatly into two days, with no rushing and no pre-dawn alarms. There's time to sit over coffee and time to wander the evening market.

blocks.html: If all you have is a weekend, Udon Thani fits nicely into 2 days and 1 night. Spend the first day taking it easy in town with no long drives, eat well, and walk Nong Prajak in the cool evening air. On the second day you head out to Ban Chiang, about 55 kilometers away, a little over an hour's drive. A half-day in the morning wraps it up well, and you're back in the city in time for lunch before moving on.

This plan is written for self-driving (rental or your own car), because there's no convenient direct public transport to Ban Chiang. If you don't have a car, you can hire a van or a taxi for the whole second day, roughly 1,500–2,000 THB per day depending on what you agree on.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Udon city center + Nong Prajak in the evening

blocks.html: No need to rush on the first day. Start with a Vietnamese breakfast, which this city is known for, since Udon has had a long-established Thai-Vietnamese community. Pho, khao piak sen (rice noodle soup), and fresh spring rolls are easy to find and genuinely good. After that, take in the city spots at an easy pace and close the day at Nong Prajak when the sun softens.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: In town · easy walking, no long drives

items.note: Pho, khao piak sen, fresh spring rolls. There are several Vietnamese breakfast shops in the municipal area, around 40–80 THB a plate. Finish with a Vietnamese coffee.
A quick stop to pay respects. The Pu-Ya Shrine beside the lake is pretty and shaded, with a small Chinese garden that's good for photos.
Housed in the old Rajinuthit building, it tells the story of the city and Prince Prachak. Free entry, nicely air-conditioned, a good way to escape the midday heat.

items.activity: Lunch — kuay jab yuan or Isan food
items.note: Kuay jab yuan, with chewy rolled noodles in a clear broth, is an Udon specialty. Or go for som tam, grilled chicken, and laab, all easy to find around town. Around 50–70 THB a bowl.

items.activity: Check in at the hotel, rest up
items.note: Most in-town hotels are near Nong Prajak and UD Town, within walking distance of the evening market.
The loop around the lake is over 3 kilometers. Walk or cycle in the breeze and check out the giant yellow ducks in the middle of the water, the city's signature photo spot.
In the evening plenty of stalls open around the lake, with snacks and homemade coconut ice cream. A relaxed spot to sit and catch the breeze.

items.activity: Dinner at UD Town or the night market
items.note: UD Town sits next to the train station and stays open until 10 pm. It's an open-air mall with street food and an air-conditioned food court, reasonably priced, with shopping to round out the evening.

blocks.title: Day 1 tip
blocks.html: Nong Prajak is at its best around 16:30–18:30, when the heat eases off, the breeze picks up, and there's a good crowd. Come at midday and it's hot with the stalls still closed, so it's worth avoiding.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Ban Chiang World Heritage, then back to town

blocks.html: On the second day you head out of town to Ban Chiang in Nong Han district, about 55 kilometers away, a little over an hour's drive along Highway 22 (Udon–Sakon Nakhon) before turning off toward Ban Chiang. This is a prehistoric site over 4,000 years old, listed as a World Heritage site back in 1992. The museum is well laid out and pleasantly cool inside.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Ban Chiang · a half-day morning wraps it up well

items.note: A light kai krata (pan-fried eggs) or congee before you set off. There are gas stations and coffee shops along the way to stop at.

items.activity: Drive out of town to Ban Chiang
items.note: Highway 22 is a good road and an easy drive, about 55 km, a little over an hour.

Open 09:00–16:00 (usually closed Monday–Tuesday, check before you go). Entry is around 30 THB for Thais, 150 THB for foreigners. It displays the painted pottery and Bronze Age finds the site is famous for.

items.activity: Wat Pho Si Nai excavation pit
items.note: Inside Ban Chiang village, a short walk from the museum. It's a real excavation pit where you can see skeletons and pots left in their original positions.
Ban Chiang has its signature painted pottery, woven cloth, and handmade crafts at friendly prices. A nice way to support the community.
Several Isan restaurants in the village serve som tam, grilled fish, and laab, around 50–80 THB a dish.
You'll reach town around 3 pm. Stop for souvenirs like moo yor, naem, and Chinese sausage before heading home or returning the car.

blocks.title: Check before you go to Ban Chiang
blocks.html: The museum is often closed on Monday and Tuesday. If your trip falls on those days, swap Ban Chiang to the first day or shift it to a Wednesday–Sunday so you don't waste the trip. Entry fees and hours can change, so calling the museum ahead is the safest bet.

blocks.text: Food you shouldn't miss on this plan

blocks.html: Udon is a real food town. What sets it apart is Vietnamese food and kuay jab yuan, alongside punchy Isan dishes. Here's what to make room for on a 2-day trip.

items.name: Kuay jab yuan
items.blurb: Chewy rolled noodles in a clear broth with minced pork, egg, and meatballs, topped with fried shallots. It's the dish people come to Udon for, well balanced and not over-seasoned.

items.name: Vietnamese pho
items.blurb: Flat rice noodles in a bone broth fragrant with spices, with beef or meatballs, eaten with fresh herbs and Vietnamese-style dipping sauce. A satisfying breakfast.

items.name: Khao piak sen
items.blurb: Chewy noodles made from rice flour in a hot broth with minced pork and a poached egg. A light Vietnamese-style breakfast that Udon does well.

items.name: Naem nueang
items.blurb: Grilled pork wrapped in rice paper with fresh herbs and rice vermicelli, dipped in Vietnamese-style sauce. A fun set to assemble yourself, great for sharing.

items.name: Som tam, grilled chicken & laab
items.blurb: Classic, boldly flavored Isan food: som tam with fermented fish and crab, charcoal-grilled chicken, and dry-roasted pork laab. Easy to find all over town, tasty and cheap.

items.name: Kai krata & loaded toast
items.blurb: An easy breakfast the lakeside shops at Nong Prajak do well: a hot pan of eggs with pork sausage, eaten with crisp bread. Light on the wallet.

items.name: Moo yor, naem & Chinese sausage
items.blurb: The city's go-to souvenirs: firm moo yor, nicely tangy naem. Buy some to take home or snack on along the way. Souvenir shops are all over town.

items.name: Homemade coconut ice cream
items.blurb: A coconut ice cream shop by Nong Prajak with a cute setting and photo corners. A cool dessert to end the evening after a walk around the lake.

blocks.text: Where to stay, parking, and budget

blocks.html: Staying in town is best for this plan, since you can walk to Nong Prajak and UD Town, and it's an easy early start out to Ban Chiang. Mid-range hotels in town run 600–1,200 THB a night, with plenty to choose from.

items: Where to stay — pick the area around Nong Prajak or near UD Town so you can walk to eat and explore without driving at night.
Parking — UD Town and Nong Prajak have parking, and the Ban Chiang museum has a free lot.

Budget per person for 2 days — hotel split two ways is about 400–600 THB, food for 4–5 meals around 500–700 THB, Ban Chiang entry 30 THB, fuel/hired car depending on your group. Roughly 1,200–1,800 THB per person all in.
Best season — good year-round. If you also want to add the Red Lotus Sea, come December–February and arrive before 10 am, when the lotuses are in full bloom across the lake.

blocks.text: Want to add another half-day? What to tack on

blocks.html: If you set off early or have time left on the second day, you can add one more stop. Each option heads in a different direction, so picking one near your way home makes the best use of your time.

items.name: Red Lotus Sea (Kumphawapi)
items.blurb: A lake covered in red lotuses. Take a boat out in the morning before 10 am; it's only at its best December–February, south of the city.

items.name: Kham Chanot
items.blurb: A famous sacred site, the Naga's palace, that draws big crowds and queues. It's in Ban Dung district, well to the north, so set aside a half-day.

items.name: Wat Pa Phu Kon (Na Yung)
items.blurb: A white marble reclining Buddha in the forest, beautiful and quiet. It's far to the north, best for those with a car and a full day.

items.name: Udon Thani City Museum
items.blurb: If you didn't stop by on day one, catch it before you leave. It's in town, free, and takes about an hour.

faq.q: What can you do in Udon Thani in 2 days and 1 night?
faq.a: Spend the first day in town: a Vietnamese breakfast, paying respects at the Pu-Ya Shrine, the city museum, then an evening walk around Nong Prajak to see the yellow ducks, followed by the UD Town night market. On the second day, drive to Ban Chiang, the World Heritage museum, for a half-day in the morning, then head back to town in time for lunch.

faq.q: How far is Ban Chiang from Udon city, and how do you get there?
faq.a: It's about 55 kilometers, a little over an hour's drive along Highway 22. Without your own car, it's best to rent one or hire a van/taxi for the day, around 1,500–2,000 THB, since there's no convenient direct public transport.

faq.q: What are the Ban Chiang museum's hours and entry fee?
faq.a: Open 09:00–16:00, usually closed Monday and Tuesday. Entry is around 30 THB for Thais and 150 THB for foreigners; students in uniform and monks enter free. Fees and hours can change, so check with the museum before you go.

faq.q: When is the best time to walk Nong Prajak?
faq.a: In the evening, 16:30–18:30, when the heat eases off, the breeze picks up, and plenty of stalls around the lake are open. You get the walk, the yellow ducks, lakeside snacks, and the sunset. Avoid midday, when it's hot and the stalls aren't open yet.

faq.q: Can you do this plan without your own car?
faq.a: On the first day in town, walking plus a motorbike taxi or Grab works fine. For the second day to Ban Chiang, it's best to hire a van or taxi for the whole day, or rent a car and drive yourself, which is the most flexible and lets you control your own timing.
